findings.title: Negative offset slicing on Django QuerySet will raise an exception, not work as claimed
findings.body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, the code slices the queryset directly with a negative start_offset (`queryset[start_offset:stop]`). Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ explicitly disallows negative indices/slices and raises `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` The comment above this block claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' which is false. Since Cursor.from_string (sentry/utils/cursors.py) does not validate that offset is non-negative, any caller can supply a cursor string with a negative offset (e.g. `0:-5:0`) together with `optimized_pagination=true` and trigger an unhandled 500 error on this endpoint — a denial-of-service style bug for a code path meant to be a performance optimization.

findings.title: Potential AttributeError when organization_context.member is None
findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` will raise AttributeError if `organization_context.member` is None for any non-superuser request reaching this line (e.g. users accessing the org via a path that does not populate `member`). There is no None-check before accessing `.has_global_access`, so a non-superuser request could 500 instead of simply falling back to the default paginator.

findings.title: New pagination code path has no test coverage
findings.body: This PR introduces a brand-new conditional branch (triggered via the `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter) that switches to `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True` for superusers / org admins with global access. No tests were added for this branch, nor for the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` class in paginator.py (~100 new lines), despite it introducing new behavior (negative-offset handling) that can crash requests (see related finding). This is a significant test gap for security- and stability-sensitive code.

findings.title: max_segment_spans parameter is now dead/misleading configuration
findings.body: The `max_segment_spans` constructor parameter (default 1001) is no longer referenced anywhere in buffer.py after this change — the span-count limiting logic that previously used it in `_load_segment_data` (checking `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`) has been removed and replaced by a hardcoded cutoff of 1000 inside `add-buffer.lua` (`zpopmin` when `span_count > 1000`). Any caller setting a custom `max_segment_spans` value now has zero effect, and the hardcoded Lua threshold (1000) is inconsistent with the old default (1001), making the parameter dead and misleading.

findings.title: Silent span eviction with no metrics/logging, changing failure mode from 'drop whole segment' to 'silently truncate'
findings.body: Previously (in Python, `_load_segment_data`), when a segment exceeded `max_segment_spans`, the whole segment was dropped and a metric (`spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded`) plus an error log were emitted, making this clearly observable. Now the eviction happens inside the Lua script via `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`, silently discarding the oldest-scored (earliest end_timestamp) spans whenever a segment exceeds 1000 entries, with no corresponding metric or log anywhere in the codebase. This is a data-integrity/observability regression: oversized segments are now silently truncated instead of being flagged, and operators have no way to detect how often or how severely this occurs.

findings.title: Redirect lookup depth limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without updated rationale
findings.body: The loop bound for following redirect chains was reduced from 10000 to 1000, and the explanatory comment ('theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') was deleted entirely rather than updated. The same correctness caveat still applies at the new, much smaller bound, meaning very deep segment/span trees (depth > 1000) are now substantially more likely to fail to be joined correctly than before, and there is no comment documenting this trade-off for future maintainers.

findings.title: Unrelated, under-reviewed feature bundled into a PR about span-buffer eviction
findings.body: This PR's title/description describe an optimization to span buffer insertion/eviction, yet the bulk of the diff (OptimizedCursorPaginator, the new `optimized_pagination` endpoint branch, and the Cursor negative-offset comment) is an unrelated pagination feature exposed to privileged users with dubious safety claims ('This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level') that does not actually prevent the negative-offset crash described in another finding. Bundling a large, untested, security-adjacent feature into a PR ostensibly about Redis Lua script changes makes this hard to review properly and should be split out or justified separately.
